transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Meeting: Escalation Playbook v2 — severity + triggers + comms cadence (Support/CS/SRE sync)
Recorded: 2026-02-18 5:00 PM PT
Duration: 53 min
Organizer: Dev Patel

Attendees:
- Dev Patel (Director, Customer Support)
- Jasmine Liu (VP Customer Success)
- Sean Gallagher (Director of SRE)
- Rafael Mendes (SRE, oncall/escalation owner)
- Owen Phillips (Support Engineering)
- Priya Shah (Support Engineering, known-issues validation)
- Rachel Kim (Enterprise CS)
- Chris Osei (Product Ops)
- Tomáš Novák (SRE, runbooks/paging hygiene)
- Miles Thornton (Incident automation)

Auto Summary (generated)
- Team aligned on a single severity scale mapping (P0–P4 / Sev0–Sev3) and clarified that "severity" is based on customer impact, not effort.
- Agreed escalation triggers for common failure modes: elevated 5xx/timeouts, streaming disconnects, 429 throttling spikes, Dedicated capacity shortfalls/latency spikes, and Private SSO/SAML outages.
- Confirmed customer comms update cadence by tier, and that status page posts are reserved for multi-customer incidents / widespread impact.
- SRE requested tighter gating to protect paging hygiene; Support requested clear "when to page" vs "when to file" rules and a minimum-info checklist.

Topics
1) Severity definitions (P0–P4) and mapping to incident process
2) Escalation triggers by failure mode (Hosted/Dedicated/Private)
3) Customer comms cadence: first response + update frequency + what we can promise
4) After-hours: when we engage oncall, what is not an emergency
5) Action items + owners

Questions captured
- Do we treat "single enterprise tenant down" as incident-level (status page?) or private comms only?
- For 429s, what thresholds indicate platform issue vs customer misconfig?
- For streaming drops, do we page SRE on rate spikes even if retries recover?

Transcript

[00:00] Dev Patel: Cool, I think we’re live. Thanks everyone. Goal today is basically to get to a final cut on severity matrix plus escalation triggers and then the comms update cadence so Support and SRE aren’t, like, arguing in the moment.

[00:18] Jasmine Liu: And we need this to be shippable. Like, Confluence page is fine, but it has to be unambiguous for tiered customers.

[00:26] Sean Gallagher: +1. Also, please, paging hygiene. I know everyone wants faster engagement, but if everything is a page then nothing is.

[00:39] Dev Patel: Yep. So, starting point: P0 to P4. We’ve been mixing Sev0/Sev1 language from incident process. I propose: we keep Support-facing P0–P4, and we map to incident Sev0–Sev3 when it becomes an incident.

[00:55] Rafael Mendes: That’s fine. But the key is: what is the trigger to jump from “support escalation” to “oncall page” to “declare incident.” Those are three different things.

[01:06] Owen Phillips: And Support needs a clear rule for the first two at least. Right now people are paging for stuff that’s basically “customer has aggressive timeouts.”

[01:17] Dev Patel: Right. So severity definition first: P0 is “production down” or “material outage” for a tiered customer, or multi-customer platform regression. P1 is major degradation, partial outage, severe latency, lots of 5xx but not total.

[01:34] Rachel Kim: Can we define “material” in a way that’s consistent for enterprise? Like, if an enterprise is running a launch and they’re missing an SLA, they will call it P0.

[01:45] Jasmine Liu: “Material” needs to be: can’t serve end users, or critical business workflow is blocked, not “my p95 went up.” But for Dedicated, if they have reserved throughput and they cannot hit it, that’s pretty severe.

[02:01] Sean Gallagher: I’d rather tie it to objective signals. Like error rate, timeouts, or inability to authenticate. Latency is tricky because it can be customer prompt changes too.

[02:13] Chris Osei: Sorry, quick one: are we still using P0–P4 for reporting? Or do we want to normalize into Sev? It matters for dashboards.

[02:21] Dev Patel: Support and CS will use P-levels. Incident tool uses Sev-levels. We’ll just map them in the table for reporting.

[02:29] Chris Osei: Got it.

[02:31] Dev Patel: Okay, examples. P0 examples: elevated 5xx across a region for hosted, like “eu-west returns 500 for 30% of requests.” Or SSO down for a Private customer, nobody can log in. Or Dedicated cluster hard down.

[02:52] Tomáš Novák: I’d also add: widespread streaming failure where connections drop immediately. That’s functionally down.

[03:01] Priya Shah: On that—Support sees “streaming disconnected” errors a lot that are just mobile networks. I want the example to say “sustained spike above baseline AND reproducible from our side.”

[03:13] Rafael Mendes: Exactly. “Customer reports” is not a metric.

[03:17] Dev Patel: Yep. So triage checklist will include “can we reproduce from a Redwood canary” plus request IDs.

[03:25] Miles Thornton: And the incident-bot can enforce “request ID or trace ID” as required before posting #incidents stub.

[03:33] Dev Patel: Great. Next: P1 examples: 5xx between like 5 and 20%, or severe latency increases that breach SLA for a tiered customer for more than, say, 15 minutes.

[03:49] Sean Gallagher: “Breach SLA” implies we know their contract in real time.

[03:53] Rachel Kim: We do for Dedicated and Private. Not perfect, but we can reference tier defaults.

[03:58] Jasmine Liu: Put “breaches tier target or contract target” and link to the SLA table.

[04:06] Dev Patel: Okay.

[04:08] Owen Phillips: P2 would be: customer impacted but workaround exists. Like: 429 because they launched, we can recommend backoff and quota adjustment.

[04:19] Am— sorry, not Amara, I’m mixing names— (crosstalk)

[04:21] Dev Patel: We don’t have Amara here, but yes.

[04:25] Priya Shah: And P3/P4 are informational, doc bugs, “how do I” requests, not escalations.

[04:33] Dev Patel: Cool. Now triggers by failure mode.

[04:37] Sean Gallagher: Before triggers: we need to say: “Escalation” means engineering engagement within X time. “Paging” is reserved for oncall. Not every escalation is a page.

[04:47] Dev Patel: Agree. So: escalation types: (1) Support escalation to Eng owner async, (2) page oncall, (3) declare incident.

[04:58] Rafael Mendes: Let’s define gate for paging. For hosted: page if multi-customer, multi-project, or region-wide metric breach. For single customer: only if there’s evidence of platform defect and they’re blocked.

[05:13] Rachel Kim: For enterprise, single customer can still be huge. Like their whole app is down.

[05:18] Sean Gallagher: Fine, but then we need “minimum evidence” so we’re not chasing shadows.

[05:24] Owen Phillips: Minimum evidence is also what Support is struggling with. We don’t always ask for the right logs.

[05:32] Dev Patel: Great. We’ll add “Escalation Required Fields.” Owen, that’s your lane with INT-1337.

[05:39] Owen Phillips: Yep.

[05:40] Dev Patel: Okay, failure mode 1: 5xx.

[05:43] Rafael Mendes: Triggers: if error rate > X for Y minutes. Internally we have alerts. For Support: if the customer reports sustained 5xx and we see correlated spikes in dashboards, page oncall.

[05:55] Tomáš Novák: And if it’s a pinned model version failing, it might be model shard issue; still page if it’s widespread, otherwise route to runtime oncall? (might be the same person)

[06:05] Sean Gallagher: For practical purposes: page SRE oncall, we’ll route. Support shouldn’t guess if it’s gateway or runtime.

[06:12] Dev Patel: Good. But we’ll include ownership map in the playbook so Support knows where to file non-page escalations.

[06:20] Dev Patel: Failure mode 2: timeouts.

[06:23] Priya Shah: We need to separate client timeouts vs server timeouts. People set 10s and then complain.

[06:29] Rafael Mendes: Yep. Required fields: client timeout setting, SDK version, whether streaming, region, model, and sample request IDs.

[06:39] Jasmine Liu: For comms: we shouldn’t tell customers “it’s your fault.” We should say “we’re investigating; we see X; here are recommended settings.”

[06:49] Dev Patel: Yep, template language will be careful.

[06:52] Dev Patel: Failure mode 3: streaming disconnects.

[06:55] Tomáš Novák: SRE stance: do not page on “streaming disconnected” unless there’s a measurable spike in disconnect rate and it correlates with a deployment or region event.

[07:06] Priya Shah: Can we specify the threshold? Like, “2x baseline for 10 minutes” or something.

[07:11] Sean Gallagher: We can’t promise numbers here because baseline varies. Put “sustained, elevated above baseline on dashboard panel.” We’ll link to the panel once Allison publishes it.

[07:23] Miles Thornton: That’s in the observability PR, right? It adds streaming disconnect rate by region and model.

[07:28] Sean Gallagher: Yep.

[07:30] Dev Patel: For Support, we’ll say: first step: confirm client retry/reconnect guidance, ask for request IDs around disconnect time, confirm keepalive. If disconnects persist and we see spike, escalate.

[07:45] Owen Phillips: And we need an explicit “safe-to-share” workaround. Like: “retry with jitter, resume prompt, don’t assume stream is complete.”

[07:53] Priya Shah: We have it, but it needs review. Some of the wording is too prescriptive. We can’t say “set X to Y” if it breaks other customers.

[08:03] Dev Patel: Great, Priya, you’ll validate those workarounds.

[08:06] Dev Patel: Failure mode 4: 429 throttling.

[08:09] Rachel Kim: This is big for self-serve. We get escalations that are really “quota misunderstanding.”

[08:15] Dev Patel: We need a clear statement: 429 is not automatically an escalation. It’s usually expected behavior. Escalate only if: sudden 429 spike without traffic change, or multiple customers, or we suspect misconfigured enforcement.

[08:30] Sean Gallagher: Yes. Also, paging oncall for 429 is almost never needed unless it’s widespread. Otherwise route to gateway/rate-limit SME asynchronously.

[08:39] Tomáš Novák: And comms: we should give immediate mitigation: exponential backoff, respect Retry-After, confirm project-level limits.

[08:48] Rafael Mendes: Add: “if dedicated customer is getting 429, that’s weird.” That might be a policy issue.

[08:53] Dev Patel: Good call. Dedicated 429s should be P1/P2 depending on impact.

[09:00] Dev Patel: Failure mode 5: Dedicated latency spikes/noisy neighbor.

[09:04] Rachel Kim: This is where enterprise gets upset. They expect isolation.

[09:08] Sean Gallagher: It’s also where we get a lot of false pages. Latency spikes can be real, but it’s often workload shape changes.

[09:16] Owen Phillips: We need a Support checklist: what dashboard to check, what to ask customer, and when to engage SRE.

[09:22] Tomáš Novák: We can say: if p95 latency doubles vs last 24h and persists > 15 min AND the customer reports user impact, escalate to SRE but not page unless there’s evidence of cluster saturation or errors.

[09:37] Jasmine Liu: But if the customer is enterprise with 24/7 coverage expectation, we have to at least engage faster.

[09:44] Sean Gallagher: Engage faster doesn’t always mean page. We can have an “engineering escalation” SLA that’s quicker during business hours.

[09:51] Dev Patel: That’s the SLA table. We’ll specify “engineering engagement” vs “oncall page.”

[09:57] Dev Patel: Failure mode 6: Private SSO/SAML and networking.

[10:01] Rafael Mendes: That one’s tricky because it crosses teams: Security, Private Deployments, sometimes customer IdP.

[10:08] Jasmine Liu: It’s also sensitive. We have restricted handling, no customer identifiers in broad channels.

[10:14] Dev Patel: Right. For Private: if SSO is down, that’s P0 for that customer. Escalation goes to Private Deployments + Security owner, with a restricted Slack channel if needed.

[10:27] Sean Gallagher: And SRE is not always first responder there. Unless it’s platform auth. So routing rules matter.

[10:33] Owen Phillips: Can we put “if Private control plane auth is failing across customers” then SRE incident. If it’s single customer IdP config, that’s Support + Security but not an incident.

[10:44] Rafael Mendes: Yep.

[10:46] Dev Patel: Okay. Now comms cadence.

[10:50] Jasmine Liu: This is the part I care about. First response time and then update cadence. Customers don’t need constant spam, but they need predictability.

[10:59] Rachel Kim: Enterprise expectation is: “someone is on it” quickly, plus a meaningful update at least every hour in an outage.

[11:07] Sean Gallagher: That’s hard if we’re deep debugging. But we can provide “no new update, still investigating, next update at X.”

[11:15] Dev Patel: Exactly. We can standardize: P0 update every 30–60 minutes, P1 every 2 hours, P2 daily or per milestone. Something like that.

[11:26] Chris Osei: For reporting we should pick one cadence per tier or per severity? Otherwise it’s ambiguous.

[11:32] Dev Patel: Both. Tier modifies severity. Example: P0 for enterprise: update every 30 minutes; self-serve P0 (if it happens) maybe hourly and via status page.

[11:45] Sean Gallagher: Wait, status page. We should define when we post.

[11:48] Jasmine Liu: Status page is for broad impact. Not for “one enterprise customer down” unless it’s clearly platform-wide.

[11:56] Rafael Mendes: Agree. Otherwise we leak information. For single-tenant Dedicated issues, keep to private comms.

[12:05] Rachel Kim: But customers will ask “why isn’t this on the status page.” We need canned language.

[12:10] Dev Patel: We’ll add a template: “status page reflects widespread service issues; your issue appears isolated to your environment and we’ll keep you updated directly.”

[12:21] Jasmine Liu: Good.

[12:23] Dev Patel: After-hours coverage. Sean, can you speak to what we can commit to without breaking the oncall rotation?

[12:30] Sean Gallagher: For oncall: we page for P0 incidents and a subset of P1 with strong evidence. We do not page for P2, period. For enterprise, we can have an “engagement SLA” that means “someone will look” but not necessarily an immediate page unless it meets criteria.

[12:46] Tomáš Novák: Also recommend we pilot for two weeks. If paging volume spikes, we adjust triggers.

[12:51] Jasmine Liu: Fine, but we must communicate internally. CS cannot promise “engineer on a Zoom in 10 minutes” if we’re not.

[13:00] Dev Patel: Agreed. Rachel, you’ll help with tier language.

[13:06] Rachel Kim: Yep.

[13:07] Dev Patel: Let’s get into the concrete “when to page” bullets. I’ll propose and you all shoot holes.

[13:13] Dev Patel: Page SRE oncall when: (1) multi-customer outage suspected, (2) region-level 5xx/timeouts elevated and visible in dashboards, (3) Dedicated cluster down or severe degradation with objective metrics, (4) Private control plane auth outage affecting customer access, (5) security-related active incident (but that goes through Security).

[13:37] Sean Gallagher: Add “data integrity or leakage suspicion” as immediate page (and Security).

[13:41] Jasmine Liu: Yes.

[13:44] Dev Patel: Good.

[13:45] Rafael Mendes: And explicitly: “Do not page” for: single-customer 429 due to rate limits, doc requests, client networking issues with no platform evidence, and “latency seems slower” without request IDs.

[13:59] Owen Phillips: Also: streaming disconnect single customer with no dashboard spike.

[14:04] Dev Patel: Great.

[14:06] Miles Thornton: If we codify these as checkboxes, incident-bot can prompt: “Do you see dashboard correlation? yes/no.” If no, it can say “route as engineering escalation, not page.”

[14:18] Sean Gallagher: That’s perfect.

[14:21] Dev Patel: Okay, severity matrix nuance: “severity is impact.” “Priority” maybe is how fast we act. But we’re not introducing new words now.

[14:31] Jasmine Liu: Keep it simple. Impact drives severity, tier drives SLA.

[14:36] Dev Patel: Great. Now, minimum required fields. Owen and Rafael, can we agree on the list?

[14:43] Owen Phillips: For Hosted: org/project, region, endpoint, model name + version if pinned, timeframe, request IDs, error message, SDK + version, whether streaming, sample payload redacted.

[14:58] Rafael Mendes: Add: response headers if present (request-id header), and if they have retries enabled. Also “approx QPS” and any recent changes.

[15:07] Tomáš Novák: And “did this start after a deploy” — customer deploy or our deploy. Sometimes it’s their release.

[15:13] Priya Shah: For workarounds, we should include “try alternate region” only if it’s safe and supported. Otherwise we cause cross-region data concerns.

[15:22] Jasmine Liu: Exactly. For Private, region failover is not always possible.

[15:26] Dev Patel: Right. Workarounds must be tagged: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private.

[15:31] Chris Osei: Just to confirm: we’ll track escalations by category tags? Like streaming/429/SSO.

[15:36] Dev Patel: Yes. Known issues index uses that tagging too.

[15:40] Chris Osei: Great.

[15:42] Dev Patel: I’m going to jump to comms cadence table, because it’s where people disagree.

[15:47] Dev Patel: Proposal: For P0: first response within 15 minutes for Dedicated/Private/Enterprise during coverage hours, 30 minutes after-hours; updates every 30 minutes until mitigation, then hourly until stable. For self-serve P0 (platform outage): status page + first response via support within 1 hour.

[16:11] Sean Gallagher: “15 minutes” implies always available. I can do “acknowledge within 15” if it’s a page. But if it’s not paged, we can’t.

[16:19] Dev Patel: Then we define: first response SLA is Support, not engineering. Engineering engagement SLA is separate.

[16:26] Jasmine Liu: Yes. Customer sees Support response. We can commit Support ack quickly. Engineering engagement depends on trigger.

[16:34] Rachel Kim: But enterprise customers will ask “is engineering engaged.” We should state: “we have engaged the oncall engineer” only when it’s true.

[16:42] Dev Patel: We’ll add “what not to promise” in templates.

[16:45] Priya Shah: Please include “we are investigating” template that doesn’t say “root cause found.” People over-promise.

[16:52] Dev Patel: Yep.

[16:54] Sean Gallagher: For updates: 30 minutes is okay for P0. But we must allow “no change” updates. Also: if it’s an incident, #incidents is source of truth, and Support mirrors it.

[17:04] Dev Patel: There’s an alignment doc for that; we’ll link it.

[17:08] Miles Thornton: We can have incident-bot remind: “post customer update at hh:mm.” That reduces misses.

[17:15] Dev Patel: Great.

[17:17] Dev Patel: Let’s talk through one scenario quickly: streaming disconnects for an enterprise in us-east.

[17:24] Priya Shah: Step 1: collect request IDs and client environment. Step 2: check streaming disconnect dashboard. Step 3: if dashboard shows spike and other customers impacted, page SRE; if not, provide reconnect guidance and keep it as P2.

[17:41] Rafael Mendes: +1. And if it’s a P0 claim but no platform evidence, we can still escalate to runtime team async for investigation during business hours.

[17:50] Rachel Kim: For comms: we say “we’re seeing no broader service degradation; here’s immediate mitigation; we’re continuing to monitor and will update by X.”

[18:01] Jasmine Liu: Good.

[18:03] Dev Patel: Scenario 2: 429 spike post-launch.

[18:06] Owen Phillips: First response: explain rate limits, ask for their QPS, suggest exponential backoff, check quotas. Escalate to gateway SME only if quota looks wrong or sudden enforcement bug.

[18:20] Sean Gallagher: Definitely not a page.

[18:22] Dev Patel: Scenario 3: Private SSO failure after IdP change.

[18:26] Rafael Mendes: That is usually misconfiguration. Route to Security + Private Deployments. Page only if control plane auth service is down broadly.

[18:35] Jasmine Liu: And use restricted channels for artifacts.

[18:38] Dev Patel: Great. I think we’re aligned.

[18:41] Chris Osei: Can I ask a metrics question? We want MTTA (ack), MTTM (mitigation), MTTR (resolution). But what’s “mitigation” for 429? It’s not ours.

[18:52] Sean Gallagher: Exactly. For 429, “mitigation” is “customer has safe workaround” like backoff/quota change. So for reporting it can be “customer unblocked.”

[19:03] Dev Patel: Good. That’s consistent with known-issues deflection.

[19:07] Dev Patel: Alright, last: open questions. First: single enterprise tenant down, status page?

[19:14] Jasmine Liu: No status page unless multi-customer or platform-wide. Private comms only.

[19:19] Sean Gallagher: Agree.

[19:20] Rachel Kim: Add the canned language.

[19:23] Dev Patel: Second: thresholds for 429 platform issue vs customer.

[19:28] Tomáš Novák: If multiple orgs see 429 at normal traffic levels and dashboards show limiter saturation or misconfig, that’s platform. Otherwise customer.

[19:36] Sean Gallagher: Put it that way. Avoid a hard number.

[19:40] Dev Patel: Third: streaming drops with retries recover—page or not?

[19:45] Rafael Mendes: Not unless there’s correlated spike and customer is still materially impacted. If retries hide it, it’s a P2 and we fix in sprint.

[19:54] Priya Shah: But we still want to capture the pattern so it becomes known issue + fix.

[19:58] Dev Patel: Yes.

[20:00] Dev Patel: Okay I’m going to read out action items.

[20:03] Dev Patel: One, I will update the Confluence draft with today’s changes by Friday.

[20:08] Dev Patel: Two, Sean and Rafael will confirm the paging criteria and the “incident vs escalation” line, including after-hours.

[20:14] Dev Patel: Three, Owen will finalize required fields and map them to Jira template.

[20:18] Dev Patel: Four, Priya will validate safe-to-share workaround wording for top known issues.

[20:24] Dev Patel: Five, Miles will update incident-bot prompts to enforce required fields and remind comms cadence.

[20:31] Dev Patel: Six, Chris will draft the metrics dashboard spec.

[20:35] Dev Patel: Seven, Rachel will draft tier language and send to Jasmine.

[20:40] Jasmine Liu: And I’ll do final approval pass once those are in.

[20:44] Dev Patel: Perfect. Anything else?

[20:47] Sean Gallagher: Just reiterating: if Support pages without request IDs, we will bounce it back. Not to be jerks, but it’s the only way.

[20:55] Owen Phillips: Understood. We’ll train on it.

[20:57] Dev Patel: Cool. Thanks everyone.

[Meeting ended abruptly in transcript; side conversation not captured]
